This repo is a Flask-style framework named `tessel`. Everything is in `src/tessel/views.py`.

**Becoming a view function: `View.to_view_func(name, *args, **kwargs)`** (line 86, a classmethod; Flask's `as_view`)
- It builds an inner `view(**kwargs)` closure.
  - By default, with `init_every_request = True`, each request creates a new instance via `view.view_class(...)`.
  - If `init_every_request = False`, one shared instance is created up front.
  - Either way, the closure calls `self.run_view(**kwargs)` through `active_app.ensure_sync`.
- It applies any `cls.decorators` to the closure.
- It sets `view.view_class`, `__name__`, `__doc__`, `__module__`, `view.methods` and `view.provide_automatic_options` from the class (lines 129–134).
- `view.methods` is what route registration reads to decide which HTTP methods the rule accepts.

**Routing each method: `VerbView`** (line 138, subclass of `View`; Flask's `MethodView`)
- `VerbView.__init_subclass__` (line 165) builds `cls.methods`. It collects `GET`, `POST` and so on from each name in `http_method_funcs` (line 11) that the class defines, plus any methods inherited from base classes. It skips this if the class sets `methods` explicitly.
- `VerbView.run_view` (line 182) does the dispatch. It looks up `getattr(self, request.method.lower())` using `request` from `.globals`. A `HEAD` request falls back to `get` if there is no `head` handler. It then calls the handler with the URL kwargs through `active_app.ensure_sync`.

You then register it with `app.attach_route_rule("/counter", view_func=CounterAPI.to_view_func("counter"))`.
